title: Towards AI-assisted Academic Writing
extended_summary:
This paper investigates how AI can assist academic writing, focusing on two tasks: contextual citation recommendation and automatic introduction writing. The authors are motivated by the difficulty of scholarly writing, especially the effort required to find, validate, and integrate relevant prior work while maintaining writing flow. The paper asks whether large-language-model-based tools can generate useful support for academic authors in these tasks and how researchers perceive such support in practice.

The intervention is an AI-assisted academic writing system with two main components. First, it provides in situ citation recommendations by using the writer’s document context and cursor position, generating a fabricated citation query with an LLM and retrieving candidate papers from an OpenAlex-based corpus using SPECTER2 embeddings and reranking. Second, it generates introduction sections by identifying novel claims in a manuscript relative to cited references, summarizing those claims, and composing an introduction that situates the work in relation to canonical and recent literature. Quantitative evaluations assess citation retrieval on 1,015 citation contexts sampled from S2ORC and introduction generation on 14 NBER papers using ROUGE and LLM-based entailment checks.

The human-focused portion of the study consists of semi-structured interviews with six experienced academic researchers from the research division of a large technology company, all working in computer science-related fields. These interviews explored how researchers currently find and validate citations, what ideal citation-support tools would do, and how citation practices vary by context. This qualitative component complements the system evaluations by examining real writing workflows and user needs rather than classroom or student learning settings.

The paper concludes that AI-assisted writing can produce useful support for academic authors, especially for citation suggestion and introduction drafting, but that precision and interpretability are essential. The citation recommendation method retrieved ground-truth citations at moderate-to-strong rates depending on distractor difficulty, and most claims extracted from generated introductions were judged entailed by the originals. Interview findings suggest demand for tools that not only suggest citations but also help validate claims, scope surrounding text accurately, and contextualize references within the broader literature. The authors also note important limitations, including English-only evaluation and potential bias introduced by citation-based filtering of scholarly works.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: A generative AI academic writing system that uses LLM-based retrieval-augmented citation recommendation and LLM-based introduction generation for scholarly writing.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper presents and evaluates two components of an AI-assisted academic writing system: contextual citation recommendation within a live document editor and automated introduction writing from manuscript content and references.

findings.finding_summary: For contextual citation recommendation, the system was evaluated on 1,015 citation retrieval cases extracted from S2ORC papers. Retrieval performance varied by distractor set size and type: with random distractors, MRR=0.755 and p@1=0.612 for n=3; MRR=0.549, p@1=0.333, p@3=0.665 for n=5; and MRR=0.320, p@1=0.124, p@3=0.348, p@5=0.500 for n=10. Performance was somewhat lower with semantically harder distractors, but the system still retrieved ground-truth citations above chance across conditions.
findings.measure: Citation recommendation retrieval metrics: mean reciprocal rank (MRR), precision@1, precision@3, precision@5 on 1,015 contextual citation retrieval cases

findings.finding_summary: For introduction generation, text overlap evaluation on 14 NBER papers yielded an average ROUGE score of 29.9. The paper reports that generated introductions scored better when the original introduction stayed focused on a single topic.
findings.measure: ROUGE score comparing generated versus original introductions

findings.finding_summary: In LLM-based entailment evaluation of introduction generation, 52 claims were extracted from 14 generated introductions and 47 of 52 were judged entailed by the original introductions, indicating high precision. Example paragraph-level entailment scores ranged from 0.983 for a high-performing case to 0.279 for a lower-performing case.
findings.measure: LLM-based claim entailment of generated introduction claims against original introductions
findings.effect_size: 47/52 claims entailed; example entailment scores=0.983 and 0.279

quality_tier_rationale: The paper includes quantitative evaluations and qualitative interviews, but it is not an RCT, QED, or meta-analysis, and outcomes are primarily system-performance and text-quality measures rather than causal learner-impact evidence.
impact_tier_rationale: Results are promising but reported as retrieval metrics, ROUGE, and entailment rates without standardized educational effect sizes or direct student learning gains, so overall educational impact remains unclear.
